newsitem.title: MEXICO: Newest Mexican rebel group takes to the Internet.
newsitem.headline: Newest Mexican rebel group takes to the Internet.

text.p: Mexico's newest guerrilla movement, the Marxist Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR), has launched an offensive in cyberspace.

The EPR, which sprang up last year vowing to lead a mass revolt to topple the government, now broadcasts details of its struggle to Internet surfers on the World Wide Web. Its home page called "The Insurgent" features a yellow lightning bolt and a picture of hooded EPR members armed with automatic weapons reading their revolutionary manifesto in the southwestern state of Guerrero last June 28.
"The Insurgent is an effort to improve the clarity of the Mexican people in the revolutionary democratic struggle," says the editorial of the site at http://www.xs4all.nl/insurg/.
Links lead to EPR manifestoes and communiques and a series of interviews with underground rebel leaders.

The EPR has been vigorously pursued by the government since it organised a series of attacks and ambushes in which more than 30 people died. Around 200 alleged members have been arrested, but few have been convicted.

The last item on the EPR Web page index is a rebel poem dedicated to journalists that scorns the all-too-frequent Mexican scribe who lives off government bribes. "Mercenaries at the end of the day, publishers of calumny and intrigue who charge by the piece," the poem says of them.

The EPR site sits on a server run by XS4ALL, a Dutch Internet service provider. Although it appeared to have been created last year, the site passed unnoticed in Mexico until Friday, when the Mexican daily Reforma drew attention to it.

By the standards of other Latin American guerrilla Web sites, the EPR's effort appeared amateurish. Peru's MRTA offers surfers clicking on http://burn.ucsd.edu/ats/mrta.htm a video clip of the rebel group's seizure of the Japanese embassy in Lima last Dec. 17 and copious colour photos.

Mexico's Zapatista rebels in the southern state of Chiapas -- early pioneers in rebel use of the Web -- allow followers to click on links to send protest letters to Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, donate money and join peace encampments. Their site at http://www.ezln.org is trilingual, featuring French and English translations as well as original Spanish.

The EPR pages are almost all slabs of black and white text without illustration or links to other sites. They feature one black and white photograph and two simple graphics -- one of the lightning bolt and another of a gray-black bird, apparently intended as a dove of peace.
No material was visible from this year on the site, suggesting that it had not been updated for some time.
